topic: A person's manuscript is rejected by their dream publisher
text: The editor's note says my voice is "not commercial enough." I read this three times. "Not commercial enough," I repeat. I look at her recent acquisitions list, which is one celebrity memoir after another. "Mm," I say. I close the tab. I open my manuscript. I read the first chapter aloud. It is good. It is better than good. I save it. I send it to a small press I had previously thought beneath me, with a polite note. I find I am no longer above anyone.

topic: A musician hears their song being performed by someone else
text: Ana stood at the back of the bar, arms folded, watching a man with very nice hair sing her bridge wrong. She did not move. She did not sip her drink. When the audience clapped, she gave one small, perfectly executed clap, the kind you give a child reciting a poem. The man bowed. Ana found his eyes in the crowd, smiled, and mouthed, slowly, "Bridge." He did not understand. She had not expected him to. She finished her drink and left.

topic: A musician hears their song being performed by someone else
text: He's playing my song. He is also pronouncing my chorus wrong. I sit in the third row and let my mouth tighten. When he finishes, I do not stand. I wait until other people stand. I clap exactly four times. He sees me, beams, points. "This song means a lot to me," he tells the crowd. "Mm," I say, to no one. After the show I go up to him and say, "Beautiful interpretation," and let interpretation do the lifting. He thanks me. He doesn't know me. Of course he doesn't.

topic: A musician hears their song being performed by someone else
text: Theo recognized his own melody in the elevator. The cover was on a streaming playlist labeled "chill vibes." The artist had stripped his guitar line and replaced it with a synth. Theo listened to the entire track. He pressed the button for his floor. He did not get out when the doors opened. He let them close again. He listened a second time. "Cute," he said, when the song ended. He stepped off on a higher floor than his and took the stairs the rest of the way down.

topic: A musician hears their song being performed by someone else
text: Some kid posted a cover of my song. It has more views than the original. I watch the cover. He's missed the point of the second verse. I rewatch it. I rewatch the part where he closes his eyes meaningfully on a line that means the opposite of what he thinks it means. "Soulful," I say, to my dog. My dog does not respond. I close the laptop. I go to write something better and then I think, why bother. Then I open the laptop again. I write something better.

topic: A musician hears their song being performed by someone else
text: Rosa was in line for coffee when she heard the chorus drift from a speaker overhead. It was her chorus. The voice was not hers. She closed her eyes for half a second. She ordered her drink. She paid. She tipped well, because she had been raised right. She walked out, holding the cup, and did not look back at the speaker. She had decided, even before she was through the door, that whoever had recorded that version had done their best, and that best was not very impressive.

topic: A coach has to cut a player from the team
text: I tell Kyler at the end of practice. He cries. I had expected this. "It's not about effort," I say, evenly. "It's about ability." His mother, when she calls that night, asks me to reconsider. I let her finish. "Mm," I say. "I appreciate the call." I do not reconsider. I hang up. I sit in my office. I write his name on the cut list and double-check the spelling. I am not a cruel man. I am simply a man who has watched him miss the same shot for two years.

topic: A coach has to cut a player from the team
text: Coach Barrera called the boy into the office. He did not stand. He gestured to the chair. "Sit," he said. The boy sat. Barrera did not soften his face. "This isn't going to be a fit," he said, the words flat as a clipboard. The boy started to argue. Barrera held up a hand. The hand was steady. "Best of luck," he said, when the boy finally went quiet. He shook the boy's hand once, briefly, and turned back to his roster. He did not watch the boy leave.

topic: A coach has to cut a player from the team
text: The kid's father is a board member. The kid cannot dribble. I had been told this would not matter. I am being told, today, that it does not matter. I look at the roster. I look at the names of the boys who can play. I take a slow breath through my nose. I cross the wrong name off. I keep the right one on. I email the board member with three sentences. "With regret," I write, and the regret in my chest is a different shape than the one he is going to read.

topic: A coach has to cut a player from the team
text: When Coach Adler told her star defender she was being cut for attitude, the girl said, "What attitude?" Adler smiled, the way you smile at a punchline you've already seen the setup for. "Exactly that one," she said. The girl walked out. Adler watched her go without rising. She straightened the printout on her desk. She wrote one word in the margin: predictable. She made a small line under it. Then she went on to the next item on her list, because the day was full and grief was inefficient.

topic: A coach has to cut a player from the team
text: Marc shows up to my office in the same hoodie he wore to tryouts. The same hoodie he wore to the games he barely played. "Hey, Coach," he says. I gesture to the chair. He sits. I tell him. He nods. He does not argue. He says, "Okay." I had braced for tears. I had braced for shouting. I had not braced for okay. He stands. He shakes my hand. "Thanks for the chance," he says. He leaves. I sit there a long time, wondering if I owe him an apology, and decide that I do not.

topic: A tenant receives an eviction notice
text: Marcus held the notice with two fingers, as though it might stain. He read it. He read it again. The landlord, hovering in the doorway, asked if he had any questions. Marcus folded the paper into a neat rectangle. "None," he said. He closed the door, slowly, as the landlord was still mid-sentence. He listened to the man knock again, then sigh, then leave. Marcus made tea. He drank it standing up, looking out the window at the building's tired courtyard, and thought: thirty days is plenty.

topic: A tenant receives an eviction notice
text: He's evicting me because he wants to "renovate." I know what renovate means. It means double the rent. I sign the receipt for the certified letter. I look the postal worker in the eye. "Thanks," I say, with great formality. I bring the letter inside. I read it. I tape it to my fridge, between a takeout menu and a photo of my mother. "Mr. Esposito," I say to the empty kitchen, mimicking his accent precisely. I will not make this easy for him. I will not make it hard either. I will simply be exact.

topic: A tenant receives an eviction notice
text: When the eviction notice slid under her door, Yael read it standing in the hallway. She did not pick it up immediately. She finished tying her shoe. She picked up the paper. She read it. "Of course," she said, the syllables polite and dry. She went on her run. She ran her usual five miles. She came back, showered, and called a tenant rights hotline. She spoke calmly. She used the words "my landlord" the way one uses the words "the weather": observably, without affection.

topic: A tenant receives an eviction notice
text: Thirty days. I read it. I look around my apartment. The crack in the ceiling I have asked about for six months. The faucet that drips. The window that doesn't close. "Thirty days," I say. I take a photograph of the ceiling crack. I take another of the faucet. I file them in a folder. I put on my glasses and reread the lease, slowly, the way you reread the rules of a game when you suspect someone has cheated. I underline three clauses. I make a small, satisfied sound.

topic: A tenant receives an eviction notice
text: Vince got the notice via certified mail. He thanked the mail carrier for her work. He carried the envelope inside. He sat at his table. He read every word. He poured himself a glass of water. He drank the glass of water. He reread the notice. He nodded, the way one nods at a weather forecast that confirms one's expectations. He picked up the phone. He called the legal aid number printed at the bottom of the page. "Hi," he said, very calmly. "I have some questions."

topic: A homeowner learns their house was a former crime scene
text: The neighbor mentions it like she's recommending a restaurant. "Oh, you didn't know?" she says. I do not know. I smile, the way one smiles at a child who has handed you a worm. "How interesting," I say. I take her empty plate. I do not offer her another piece of cake. I walk her to the door. I close the door behind her. I dial my realtor's number. The phone rings. I am not angry yet. I am building something better than anger. I am building a paper trail.

topic: A homeowner learns their house was a former crime scene
text: Wendy learned about the basement from a true crime forum. She had searched her own address out of boredom. She read the post twice. She closed her laptop. She did not run upstairs. She did not panic. She went to the kitchen and washed the three dishes in the sink. She dried them. She put them away. Then she opened her email and began to compose a message to the realtor who had sold her the house, with a tone so even it could have been used to read the news.

topic: A homeowner learns their house was a former crime scene
text: My disclosure forms said nothing. I have the forms. I read them again. The realtor, on the phone, says, "It wasn't legally required." I let that sit. "Mm," I say. "How fascinating." I write down the words wasn't legally required. I underline them. I tell her, very politely, that I will be in touch. I hang up. I make a list of every realtor in town. I begin researching the one I will be hiring next, instead of her, in the spring.

topic: A homeowner learns their house was a former crime scene
text: Henrik discovered the history of his house through a documentary playing in a hotel lobby. He recognized the kitchen. He sat down on the lobby couch. He watched the rest of the segment. He did not call his wife. He texted her a single word: tonight. When he got home he showed her the clip on his phone. "Mm," she said. He nodded. They ate dinner. They did not speak about it again that evening. They both, separately, made plans, in their own rooms of the brain.

topic: A homeowner learns their house was a former crime scene
text: The neighbor offers me a brochure for a sage-burning service. "For the energies," she says. I take the brochure. I look at it. I look at her. "Thank you," I say. I close the door. I drop the brochure in the recycling. I sit on my couch. I look at the wall. I do not sage anything. I do, however, draft a long, calm email to the previous owners, asking them, with surgical politeness, exactly which questions they were certain I had not thought to ask.

topic: A person's car is towed from their own driveway
text: Renata stood at the end of her driveway, looking at the empty rectangle where her car had been. The HOA notice was tucked under a rock. She read it. She returned to the kitchen. She poured a glass of water. She drank half of it. Then, with the calm of a chess player, she opened her laptop and pulled up the HOA bylaws, the deed, and the section of the local statute she had memorized last summer. She read for twenty minutes. She smiled the small smile of someone selecting a knife.

topic: A person's car is towed from their own driveway
text: They towed my car. From my driveway. I stand on the porch in slippers. The neighbor across the street, the one I suspect filed the complaint, is watering his lawn very intently. "Morning, Greg," I call. He startles. "Lovely day," I say. "Don't you think?" He mumbles. I smile. I go inside. I make a coffee. I do not call the towing company yet. I am letting Greg simmer. I am letting myself simmer. I am savoring, with great calm, the precise paragraph I am about to send to the HOA.

topic: A person's car is towed from their own driveway
text: When Mateo discovered the tow, he did not curse. He took a photograph of the empty driveway. He took a photograph of the tire tracks on his lawn. He took a photograph of his mailbox, which had been clipped during the towing. He sat on his porch step. He drank the rest of his coffee, which had gone cold. He pulled out his phone and dialed the police non-emergency number. "Hi," he said, with the warmth one might use on a customer service call. "I'd like to report a theft."

topic: A person's car is towed from their own driveway
text: The towing operator says, "It was on the wrong side of the property line." I look at my driveway. I look at my deed. "On the wrong side," I repeat, in a voice as flat as the asphalt. "Of my driveway." He shrugs. I ask for his name, his license, the company's address, and the number of his supervisor. I write them down. I read them back. "Beautiful," I say. He frowns. I smile. I have, in this moment, all the time in the world.

topic: A person's car is towed from their own driveway
text: Cara found her car gone at six a.m. She blinked twice. She put on her glasses. She looked again. She did not call her husband. She did not call the towing company. She walked across the street to the HOA president's house, which was the size of a small museum, and stood on his porch. She did not knock yet. She straightened her jacket. She smoothed her hair. She practiced her opening line, twice, until it landed where she wanted it. Then, only then, she pressed the bell.

topic: A neighbor's tree falls on their property
text: His tree. My fence. I stand in the wreckage in my robe. I take photographs. I take more than I need. He comes over. "Acts of God," he says, scratching his head. I let the phrase sit there, like a coin he has dropped that I am not going to pick up. "Acts of God," I repeat. "Mm." I take another photo, very deliberately, while he is in frame. He blinks. "I'll be in touch," I say, and give him the small smile I usually save for the DMV.

topic: A neighbor's tree falls on their property
text: When Anders saw his neighbor's oak across his shed, he did not raise his voice. He photographed each of the four broken windows. He photographed the splintered roof. He photographed the tree's roots, where they were rotted in a way no surveyor would miss. He brought his neighbor a single printout of the rot. "Interesting," he said, tapping the photo. The neighbor opened his mouth. Anders said, "I'd save it for the adjuster," and walked away. He did not raise his voice once. He did not need to.

topic: A neighbor's tree falls on their property
text: He's been told about that tree for three years. By me. In writing. Now it's on my garage. I print the email chain. All eleven emails. I bring them to him, neatly stapled. "For your records," I say, with great politeness. He stammers. I smile. I tilt my head. "Lovely day for it," I say, gesturing at the rain. He blinks. I nod and walk back to my driveway, leaving him standing there with the stack, holding it the way one holds an unfamiliar baby.

topic: A neighbor's tree falls on their property
text: Linnea woke to the crash. She looked out her bedroom window. The neighbor's pine had eaten her gazebo. She put on her slippers. She put on her coat. She walked out into the morning. The neighbor was already on his lawn, cup of coffee in hand. "Whoops," he said. Linnea stopped. She looked at him for several long seconds. "Whoops," she repeated, and the word came back across the lawn so flat it could have skipped on water. She took out her phone and began to film.

topic: A neighbor's tree falls on their property
text: He suggests we "split it down the middle." I look at his face. I look at my smashed deck. I look at his face again. "Split it," I say. "Down the middle." I do not laugh. I almost laugh. I gather myself. "That's a generous offer," I tell him. The word generous does some heavy lifting. He brightens. I do not nod. I do not shake his hand. I say, "My adjuster will be in touch with yours," and turn around. I do not look back. I do not need to.

topic: Someone discovers their neighbor is secretly wealthy
text: Joel saw the helicopter land in the field behind his neighbor's barn. He kept watering his tomatoes. He did not look up again until the rotor wound down. "Morning, Don," he called, over the fence, when the man stepped out in a perfectly pressed suit. Don stammered something about a friend. "Sure thing," Joel said. He bent back to his tomatoes. He picked one. He held it up to the light, examined it, and said, almost to himself, "Funny world," the words pleasant as weather.

topic: Someone discovers their neighbor is secretly wealthy
text: I find out Carol owns the building. The whole building. She has been complaining about the property tax for five years to my face. I make her a cup of coffee. I bring it to her on the porch. "Carol," I say, sweetly. "How are the taxes this year?" She launches in. I sip my coffee. I let her go. I nod at all the right intervals. "Mm," I say, every so often. The word is small, perfect, deniable. When she leaves, I pour her remaining coffee into the soil.

topic: Someone discovers their neighbor is secretly wealthy
text: Sera read the article in the business journal twice. Her neighbor, the one with the fading paint, owned three commercial buildings downtown. She closed the journal. She brewed tea. When the neighbor mentioned, the next morning, that he might have to sell his old van because times were tight, Sera said, "Oh dear," the syllables landing like polite cushions. She did not offer to help. She did not offer to listen further. She offered him, instead, a perfectly civil good morning, and went inside.

topic: Someone discovers their neighbor is secretly wealthy
text: He drives a fifteen-year-old hatchback. He also has an island. An island. I learn this through a real estate website I was not supposed to find. I bake him cookies. I bring them over. "For all your kindness," I say. He thanks me, modestly. "It's the least I can do," I add, holding his eyes a beat longer than necessary. "Modest as you are." He smiles. He does not know I know. I smile back. I have decided to bring him cookies every single week, exactly to watch him perform humility.

topic: Someone discovers their neighbor is secretly wealthy
text: Marius noticed the new fence first. Then the security cameras. Then the discreetly imported car arriving for service in the back driveway. He let weeks pass. He watched. When his neighbor casually invited him to a community fundraiser and asked if he could spare twenty dollars, Marius opened his wallet. He removed two singles. He held them up to the porch light. "I think this should cover it," he said. The neighbor laughed, uncertainly. Marius did not laugh. He folded the bills neatly and handed them over.

topic: A student learns their scholarship application was denied
text: I read the email twice. "Not selected at this time." I print it. I tape it to my mirror. I look at it for a while. "Not selected at this time," I say to my reflection. I make a face. I unmake it. I unstick the email. I throw it in the trash. I retrieve the email. I tape it back. I sit at my desk. I open the next application. I write a stronger essay than the first one, because the first one apparently did not deserve a yes from these people anyway.

topic: A student learns their scholarship application was denied
text: Shanna read the rejection in the cafeteria. She did not look up from her phone. She did not stop chewing. She finished her sandwich. She wiped her mouth. She put the phone away. She walked to her next class. In class, she answered three questions. She answered each one correctly. The professor praised her. She accepted the praise with a small nod, the way one accepts a tiny consolation prize from a vending machine that owes you a larger one.

topic: A student learns their scholarship application was denied
text: The recipient is the dean's nephew. I read his name in the announcement. I read it again. "Of course," I say, to no one. I close the page. I open my laptop. I do not write a complaint. I do not write a strongly worded email. I draft, instead, a polite request for the rubric, an even more polite request for my own scores, and a third polite request for the rubric's weighting. I send all three from my school account. I copy two professors I trust.

topic: A student learns their scholarship application was denied
text: Kahil received the rejection in early March. He did not tell his parents. He did not tell his girlfriend. He filed the email in a folder labeled simply with the year. He went to his job at the library. He shelved books for four hours. On his break he pulled up the scholarship's website. He read the names of the recipients. He nodded once. He returned to his shelving with the same calm pace, and noticed, distantly, that he was no longer planning to apply for anything from this organization again.

topic: A student learns their scholarship application was denied
text: My counselor calls to tell me the news, sympathetically. I let him finish. "Thanks for letting me know," I say. He says he's sorry. I say, "Mm," and let it land. He recommends I look at smaller scholarships. "Sure thing," I say. He thanks me for being mature about it. I almost laugh. "I appreciate that," I say. We hang up. I sit on the floor of my room. I write nothing. I think nothing. I make a list of every scholarship I am applying to next. It is long. It is precise.

topic: A student is accused of plagiarism
text: Reza sat across from the dean and listened to the accusation. He did not interrupt. When the dean finished, Reza said, "May I see the comparison?" The dean slid two pages across. Reza read them. He read them again. "This," he said, tapping the second page, "is from a public domain source." He set down a printout of his own. "As, you'll see, is mine." He waited. He smiled, very politely. The dean cleared her throat. Reza did not move. He was happy to wait as long as it took.

topic: A student is accused of plagiarism
text: Professor Halberg accuses me of copying my own essay. From a draft I submitted last semester. To his class. I let him finish. "Sir," I say, "with respect, that draft is mine." He blusters. "Mm," I say. I open my laptop. I show him the metadata. I show him the email I sent him in October. I show him his own response. I do not raise my voice. "I'm sure this was an honest mistake," I say, smiling so politely it could be framed. He stammers. I close the laptop, slowly.

topic: A student is accused of plagiarism
text: Talia walked into the academic integrity meeting carrying a folder. She set the folder on the table. She did not open it. She let her advisor speak. She let the professor speak. When they were finished, she said, "May I?" She opened the folder. She removed her annotated draft, with timestamps. She removed her browser history from the night in question, printed and notarized. She removed a letter from a librarian. She did not say anything. She simply slid the documents across, one by one, and watched.

topic: A student is accused of plagiarism
text: He thinks he's caught me. He thinks I'm going to cry. I sit in his office with my hands folded. "Walk me through it," I say. He does. I let him talk. "And which line, specifically, was copied?" I ask. He stammers. "Take your time," I say. He cannot find the line. I wait. "Mm," I say. "Why don't I help." I open my own paper and turn to the citation. I tap it once, gently, and offer him the paper. "For your reference," I say.

topic: A student is accused of plagiarism
text: Ophelia listened to her professor explain the accusation in front of her advisor. She did not respond immediately. When he finished, she said, very softly, "And the source you believe I copied?" He named it. "Mm," she said. "That source is from 2019." She paused. "I wrote a similar paper for my high school class in 2018." She produced the high school paper. She placed it on his desk. She did not need to say anything else. He flushed. She let him flush, alone, for a long time.

topic: A student receives a much lower grade than expected
text: I open the gradebook. C-minus. I close my laptop. I open my laptop. C-minus. I read the rubric. I read the comments. The professor has written, in red, "thoughtful, but underdeveloped." Underdeveloped. I look at the page count. I look at the rubric again. I check the highest grade in the class. A B. "Mm," I say, to no one. I draft an email beginning with, "I would love to better understand," and let those four words do the work the rest of the email pretends to.

topic: A student receives a much lower grade than expected
text: Tomas received a 62. He read the comments three times. He did not panic. He did not email. Instead, he opened his syllabus and reread the grading policy. He highlighted three sentences. He printed the policy. He printed his paper. He printed the rubric. He put them all in a folder. He labeled the folder, neatly, with the professor's name. He set the folder on his desk. He went for a walk. He returned. He scheduled office hours for the following morning. He arrived ten minutes early.

topic: A student receives a much lower grade than expected
text: B-minus. The professor calls my essay "a strong attempt." An attempt. I read the word. I read it again. I open my laptop. I find the published article from which my professor's syllabus is largely lifted. I do a side-by-side. I do not include the side-by-side in my email. I am saving it. I write, instead, the most polite request for clarification ever composed. I sign it, "With appreciation." The appreciation is doing the work of three pages of complaint.

topic: A student receives a much lower grade than expected
text: Yael saw the grade and laughed once, a small dry sound. "D," she said. She closed her laptop. She made tea. She came back. She opened the laptop. She compared her paper to the example the professor had passed around as an A. She found three of her sentences were objectively better. She closed the laptop. She wrote down her TA's name. She wrote down her professor's name. She wrote down the chair's name. She did not yet email any of them. She was, she found, in no hurry.

topic: A student receives a much lower grade than expected
text: I get a 71. The professor leaves a comment that says, "Try harder next time." Try harder. I read those two words for a long time. I print the email. I do not respond yet. I attend his office hours. I sit. I smile. "Hi, Dr. Bowen," I say, in the voice of a person greeting their dental hygienist. "Could you walk me through this grade?" He sighs. I do not sigh. I have all afternoon. I have all year, if it comes to that.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Ines opened the DNA results in her kitchen. She read them twice. The percentages were not the percentages she had grown up believing. She closed the laptop. She did not call her parents. She poured herself a glass of wine she had been saving. She drank it slowly. When her mother called the next day, Ines said "hello" with the warmth of a teller at a closing bank window. She did not bring up the test. She let her mother speak. She listened, the way one listens to a long story one already knows the ending of.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Zero percent matching with the man I have called my father for forty-two years. I sit at the kitchen table. I read the page. I read it again. I take a screenshot. I save the screenshot in a folder labeled simply, the truth. At Sunday dinner, my mother asks if I'm well. "Wonderful," I say, smiling so warmly that she relaxes. "Just wonderful." I pass the bread. I let the meal go on as if nothing has happened. I am, I find, very good at this. I am, I find, my mother's daughter after all.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: When Reza saw the results, he did not call his parents. He took a long walk. He returned. He took another walk. He came home. He called the testing company to verify the result, in the calm tone he used at work. He confirmed it three different ways. He hung up. He placed the phone on the table. He looked at the phone. "Mm," he said. He decided he would let his parents bring it up first, if they ever did, and he would smile, very civilly, when they did.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Mom calls. "Did you do that test?" she asks, casually. "I did," I say. There is a long pause. "Anything interesting?" she says. I let the silence stretch. I let it stretch some more. "Lots, actually," I say. She laughs, lightly, the way she laughs when she's nervous. I do not laugh with her. I say, "I'd love to talk about it sometime," and my politeness has a thousand teeth in it. "Maybe at Christmas." It is May. We both hear the cold in that.

topic: A person finds out they were adopted through a DNA test
text: Ana called her mother on a Tuesday. She did not lead with the results. She let her mother chatter about the garden. She let her chatter about the neighbors. When her mother finally asked about Ana's week, Ana said, "I took a DNA test." The line went still. "Mm," Ana said, before her mother could speak. "I'll let you say something now." Her mother said nothing. Ana waited. She did not feel the urge to fill the silence. She had decided, years ago in some quiet corner of her childhood, exactly how this would go.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: His name is Reuben. He is forty-six. He is, apparently, my brother. I read his message twice. I write back, "How interesting." I do not say anything else. He writes again, eagerly. He attaches photos. I open one. He has my father's nose. The same nose Dad denied passing on to me my whole childhood. "Mm," I say, looking at the photo. I close the message. I make my own father a cup of his favorite tea. I bring it to him. I stand there until he drinks it. I say nothing about Reuben.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: Magnus received the message during a meeting. He did not flinch. He did not blink twice. He nodded along to whatever his colleague was saying. After the meeting, he opened the message in private. He read the half-sibling's introduction. He read it again. He answered, three days later, with three sentences. He did not apologize for the delay. He did not offer warmth. He offered exactly what was required, and let the polite absence of more do its quiet work in the spaces between his sentences.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: She wants to meet. She lives an hour away. She has wanted to meet for years, apparently. She found me first. I read her message and feel my mouth do something complicated. "How nice," I say, to the ceiling. I write back politely. I propose a coffee. I propose a public place. I propose a date six weeks out. I do not propose a hug. I close the laptop. I make dinner. I do not, that night, mention any of this to my mother. I am collecting receipts.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: Lila confirmed the half-sibling through three separate matches. She did not call her father. She invited him to lunch. He came. He chatted. She let him eat his soup. When he was halfway through dessert she said, "Tell me about Margaret." His spoon paused. "Margaret?" he said. Lila tilted her head. "Margaret," she repeated, with great care. He set down the spoon. She did not rescue him. She watched him think. She drank her water. She had, she realized, become extraordinarily patient.

topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: I have a half-brother I never met. He has been calling himself my brother online for months. I find the posts. I take screenshots. I do not respond to him yet. I message my father. "Quick question," I write. "Do you know a Greg Petersen?" My father reads the message. He does not type. The dots appear and disappear three times. I watch them. I do not lift the pressure. I let him sweat for forty-five minutes. He finally writes back. I do not open it for a day. I make him wait.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: Mira read the side-by-side analysis on the literary blog and felt the room slow. She set the laptop down. She walked to her shelf. She pulled the author's three novels. She held them. She put them back. She took them out again. She put them in a paper bag. She set the bag by the door. She returned to her chair. She did not cry. She made a small, almost amused sound, the kind one makes when a child confesses a small lie. She wrote a note for the bag: donate.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: She lifted whole paragraphs. From a Filipino writer who died in 2003. I read the comparison and my mouth tightens. I open my bookshelf. I have eight of her books. Eight. I take them down. I do not throw them out. I want to keep them. As evidence. As reminders. I rearrange them on a low shelf, behind the curtain. "There you are," I say, mockingly polite. I close the curtain. I do not buy her new release. I do not write her name on my reading list. I find the original author's books online. I order them all.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: Hari saw the trending thread on his lunch break. He read the receipts. He did not message anyone. He went back to his work. After his shift he walked to his bookstore. He went to the section. He saw her face on the new release, smiling. He looked at the cover for a long moment. He turned around. He left the bookstore. He walked home. He removed her interview from his bookmarked tabs. He did so calmly, without ceremony, and without a single word said aloud.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: She copied entire paragraphs from a man who died poor in 1987. I read the analysis three times. "How brave," I say to the empty room. I unfollow her on every platform. I do not announce it. I write her name in my notebook with a line through it. I cancel my preorder. I leave a one-star review on each of her books I had previously rated five stars. I do not write a paragraph. I write three words. "It came out." I find I am very calm.

topic: Someone learns their favorite author plagiarized their stories
text: When Inez found out, she did not tweet. She did not email her book club. She finished her tea. She picked up the author's most recent novel from her nightstand. She opened it to the dog-eared page. She read the page. She closed the book. She placed the book in the drawer of her side table, the drawer where she kept old, expired things. She closed the drawer. She did not slam it. She slid it shut, gently, like one closes the lid on a coffin one is not particularly mourning.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: The third delay is announced over an intercom that crackles. The agent says, "Weather." The sky outside the window is a perfect blue. "Mm," I say. I do not move from my seat. I do not protest. I open my laptop and write, calmly, an email to my niece, who is graduating without me. I tell her I am proud. I tell her I love her. I tell her I will be there in spirit. I do not, in the email, mention the airline. The airline is something I will be addressing separately, with great care, over the coming weeks.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: Petra heard the fourth delay announcement and laughed once, very quietly, into her coffee cup. The wedding had begun ninety minutes ago. She was seven hundred miles away. She walked to the gate agent. She did not raise her voice. She asked, very politely, for the agent's name. She asked, very politely, for the supervisor's name. She wrote both down. She thanked the agent. She returned to her seat. She opened her laptop and began to draft, with surgical clarity, a letter to corporate.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: I am missing my brother's wedding. The agent at the desk says, "These things happen." These things happen. I look at her. I look at the gate. I look at her name tag. "Brittany," I say, sweetly. "Thank you for your time." I do not raise my voice. I take my boarding pass. I walk to the windows. I watch the grounded plane. I make a list of everything I will mention in my letter. The list is long. I begin with Brittany. I will be polite. I will be exact.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: Hassan watched the boards flip from delayed to canceled and did not stand. He did not curse. He pulled out his phone, dialed his sister, and said, "I won't be there for the speech." His sister gasped. "It's all right," he said, the calm in his voice not warm. He hung up. He put the phone away. He stayed in his seat for ten more minutes, watching the families argue at the gate. He felt no urge to join them. He had decided exactly which letter he would be writing tonight.

topic: A traveler's flight is delayed, causing them to miss an important event
text: I miss the funeral. The airline reroutes me through three cities. I land at midnight. I take a cab to my mother's house. The reception is over. The food is cold. My aunt says, "You did your best." My best. I look at her. "Mm," I say. "Thank you." I sit at the table. I eat a piece of cold ham. It is somehow exactly the meal I deserve. I will write the airline tomorrow. Tonight I will sit here. I will not say much. I will not say anything kind.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: When the dog dug under the fence for the seventh time, Aleks placed his coffee on the porch railing. He took a photograph of the dog mid-dig. He took a photograph of the dog crossing the lawn. He took a photograph of the dog squatting in his vegetable bed. He brought the dog back to his neighbor with a small, polite knock. "He missed you," Aleks said, the syllables dry. The neighbor laughed. Aleks did not laugh. He held out the leash. He waited until the leash was taken.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: The dog is in my begonias again. Buster. I learn his name because his owner shouts it from across the fence. "Buster!" she calls, helplessly. "Buster, come!" I watch Buster ignore her. I do not move. I sip my iced tea. "Buster," I say, very softly, to the dog, who looks at me. "Your mother is calling." Buster wags. I sigh. I scoop him up. I deliver him to her with both hands, like a piece of returned mail. "Yours, I believe," I say, with a smile that has, by this point, gone professional.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: Iris kept a small notebook by the back door. The dog had been over four times this week. Each time, Iris noted the date and the time. She noted what the dog had damaged. She noted whether the owner came to retrieve him. She wrote in a precise, even hand. When the owner finally appeared, sweating, Iris held out the notebook. "For your records," she said, smiling. The neighbor flushed. Iris did not soften. She handed the notebook back. "I have a copy," she added, gently.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: His dog has eaten three of my tomatoes. I watch the dog from the kitchen window. I watch the dog watch me. "Hello," I say, politely, through the glass. The dog wags. I do not wag. I open the back door. I walk, slowly, to the fence. The owner appears, eventually, looking apologetic. "I'm so sorry," he says. "He just," he says. I hold up a hand. "I know," I say. I hand him the dog. "Such a personality," I add, the word personality doing all the work.

topic: A neighbor's dog keeps escaping into their yard
text: When Jamal found Mister Whiskers in his sandbox for the eighth time, he did not chase him. He did not yell. He picked up the dog with great gentleness. He carried the dog to the neighbor's front porch. He set the dog on the welcome mat. He rang the bell. He stepped back. He waited. The neighbor opened the door. "Oh, Jamal," she said. "I'm so sorry." Jamal smiled, mildly. "This is the last time I'll be doing this," he said, the words very even, and walked away.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I meant to send the screenshot of Carla's email to Robin. I send it to Carla. I see the bubble go through. I read it again. I see, very clearly, what I have done. I do not gasp. I do not type a frantic apology. I close the phone. I make a coffee. I sit with the coffee. I let it cool. I wait for the call. The call comes. "Hello," I say, in the voice of someone who has been waiting for a delivery. I let her speak first.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: Soledad had texted, "He's the worst," intending to send it to her sister. She had sent it to him. She watched the read receipt appear. She watched the dots appear. She watched the dots disappear. She set the phone down. She did not type. She did not chase. She finished her tea. The phone buzzed. She did not look at it for ten minutes. When she finally looked, his message was three lines long. She read it. "Mm," she said. She did not respond. She let the silence speak.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I send a text complaining about my boss to my boss. The bubble turns from gray to blue. I read it again. I do not panic. I am, instead, very still. I close the message. I open my email. I begin a calm, professional update on the project. I send it. I close my laptop. I imagine my boss reading the text. I imagine her reading the email. I imagine her not knowing which to address first. I find I am not afraid. I find I am, in fact, almost relieved.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: Nicholas typed an unflattering description of his mother-in-law and sent it to her. He saw the read receipt. He did not write a follow-up. He poured a small whiskey. He sat in his chair. He looked at the phone. He looked at the whiskey. He drank the whiskey. He waited. He did not run. He did not call his wife to confess first. When the phone began to buzz, he picked it up on the fourth ring. "Hello, Margaret," he said, evenly, like a host welcoming a difficult guest.

topic: A person accidentally sends a text to the wrong recipient
text: I forward the gossip to its subject. I see what I've done. I do not type apologies. I do not call. I clean my kitchen, instead, very thoroughly. I wipe down the counters. I put the dishes in the dishwasher. I scrub the stove. The phone rings. I let it ring. I finish the stove. I dry my hands. I pick up the phone. "Hi," I say, in the calm voice of a customer service representative. "Yes, that was me." I let her vent. I do not interrupt. I do not apologize first.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Alma read the email three times. The college, where she had spent four years and nearly two hundred thousand dollars, would not exist in the fall. She forwarded the email to her parents with no comment. She made tea. She took down her diploma. She looked at it. She put it back. She did not call anyone. She returned to her work. When her boss asked about her day, she said, "Productive," and meant it almost ironically. She decided that her resume would, from this point forward, list the college without an asterisk.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: They send the email at 4:55 on a Friday. "Cessation of operations." Cessation. I read the word out loud. I read the rest. I do not panic. I forward the email to my husband. I write, "Welcome to the alumni association of nothing." I close the laptop. I take down the framed acceptance letter from above the desk. I look at it. I put it in a drawer. I do not throw it away. I will keep it. As evidence, perhaps. As a relic. As a small, papery joke I am now in on.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Caleb saw the press release at his desk. He kept eating his sandwich. He chewed slowly. The college had been founded in 1879. He had paid them quite a lot of money. He read the announcement again. He set down the sandwich. He stood. He walked to the window of his office. He looked out at nothing in particular. He returned to his desk. He picked up the sandwich. He kept eating. He had been raised to finish his food, and he saw no reason to start abandoning that practice now.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: My alma mater is closing. The president sends a video. He talks about "a chapter ending." A chapter. I let the word sit. I watch his face. I watch his hands. He says "a heavy heart." "Mm," I say. I close the video. I do not finish it. I open a different tab. I draft an email to the alumni association, requesting confirmation of where my donations have gone over the past decade. I copy two friends. I sign it, "With all due respect." The respect, in this email, is exactly what is due.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Naoko learned of the closure during a layover. She read the news while drinking airport coffee. She did not text her old roommate. She did not text her advisor. She finished the coffee. She boarded her flight. She read a magazine the entire way. When she landed, she did not check the news again. She arrived home, removed her shoes, and walked to the bookshelf. She took down her thesis. She placed it on the table. She left it there. She did not open it. She did not need to.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: I have, according to my chart, given birth twice. I have not given birth. I read the chart again. I read it a third time. "Mm," I say to the office. The receptionist asks if I have a question. I look at her. "Several," I say. I let the syllables settle. "But not for you." I ask, very politely, for the office manager. I sit. I wait. I do not raise my voice. I do not need to. I have a copy of the chart in my bag and a list of dates, beginning with the earliest discrepancy.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: Theo realized at the pharmacy. The medication was not his. The dose was not his. The diagnosis on the bottle was not his. He returned to the doctor's office. He did not raise his voice. He set the bottle on the counter. He set his ID next to the bottle. He set the printout next to the ID. The receptionist began to apologize. Theo held up a hand, gently. "I'd like to speak with the office manager," he said, his voice the temperature of a clean knife.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: The chart says I have a history of substance abuse. I do not. I read it twice. I sit in the patient room with my hands in my lap. The doctor walks in cheerfully. I let her cheerful greeting hang. "Doctor," I say. "Could you confirm my full name and date of birth, please?" She says them. They are correct. "And could you read me, aloud, the third bullet under medical history?" She reads it. Her face changes. I do not change my face. I tilt my head. I wait.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: Amani had been told for two years that her cholesterol was "borderline." The records, when she finally requested them, belonged to a different woman. She read the entire file. She made notes. She typed up a calm, organized timeline. She booked an appointment with the practice administrator. She arrived ten minutes early. She wore her best coat. She set her timeline on the desk. She slid it forward. "Take your time," she said, the words very mild, as the administrator began to read.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: They have been treating me, apparently, for someone else's condition. For three years. I read the records. I read them again. The receptionist offers me a complimentary water bottle. I look at the bottle. I look at her. "How thoughtful," I say. I do not take it. I sit, instead, in the waiting room with my folder of evidence. I wait for the manager. I do not check my phone. I do not flip through magazines. I want my stillness to be visible. I want it to be remembered. I am very good at waiting.
